idiom_name: InheritableThreadLocal plus a withContext save/set/restore helper
implementation_notes: Scala runs on the JVM and uses java.lang.ThreadLocal as its thread-local primitive, normally wrapped in an object that writes the save, set, try/finally and restore sequence once. The classic key/collection/proxy structure is replaced by the ThreadLocal instance and the JVM's per-thread map; the wrapper is where the lifetime rule lives, because Scala's default ExecutionContext runs tasks on a shared ForkJoinPool whose threads are reused and are not the request's threads. InheritableThreadLocal is the variant to reach for only when child threads created inside the work item must see the parent's value, remembering that the copy happens at thread creation only.
pitfalls: ExecutionContext threads are pooled and reused, so a value set on one task is visible to the next task scheduled on that thread - clear it in a finally and never treat a ThreadLocal as per-request state under Futures.
InheritableThreadLocal copies values when a thread is created (pooled threads are created once), so children inherit a stale parent or nothing at all, and the copy is shallow for mutable values.
A value set inside a Future is lost at the next thread switch unless the future carries an explicit context; passing the value (or a context parameter) is the recommended alternative in Scala.

variants.name: scala.util.DynamicVariable (dynamic scope on top of InheritableThreadLocal)
variants.idiom_name: DynamicVariable.withValue(thunk) with a per-thread binding stack
variants.implementation_notes: DynamicVariable gives the ambient value dynamic scope: the accessor is statically bound, the current value is pushed with withValue and automatically restored when the thunk returns, and each thread gets its own stack of bindings (the Scala 3 implementation is an InheritableThreadLocal whose initial value is the constructor parameter, and a new thread receives a copy of the parent's binding stack). It is the idiomatic choice for short-lived bindings that must not outlive the block, such as a transaction or a locale during one call. It is still thread-bound: an ExecutionContext thread created earlier has its own stack, and a value pushed inside a Future is not visible after the thread switch.
variants.code_sketch:
val current = new scala.util.DynamicVariable[RequestContext](RequestContext())

current.withValue(ctx) {          // dynamic scope: reverts when the thunk returns
  service.invoke()
}

current.value                     // current binding, per-thread stack
pitfalls: A newly created thread copies the parent's binding stack, so the parent's value can leak into unrelated child work; pooled threads created earlier never see later pushes.
withValue restores the previous value only when the thunk returns normally or throws - values pushed inside a Future are already outside the dynamic extent.
DynamicVariable is a thin wrapper over InheritableThreadLocal, so it inherits every thread-lifetime problem of the primitive it hides.
